leads.text: Emergent marsh dominated by bulrushes or spikerushes (e.g., soft stem bulrush [Scirpus validus], river bulrush [S. fluviatilis], hardstem bulrush [S. acutus], slender bulrush [S. heterochaetus], or Small's spikerush [Eleocharis smallii]). Substrate is mineral soil. Associated with wave-washed shore.
leads.rt: MRn93 Northern Bulrush-Spikerush Marsh p. 299

leads.text: Northern Floristic (FDn) Region species present (Table FD-1, p. 99). Canopy of red, white, or jack pine, or various hardwoods [almost never has bur oak]. Usually on outwash plain, moraine, or sand dune. On somewhat excessively drained to moderately well-drained, sandy forest soils or soils lacking dark surface horizons. Most common in the northeastern half of MDL.
leads.rt: If a + a' < 0 go to b

leads.text: Dry pine woodland, occasionally mixed with hardwoods. Canopy dominated by jack and red pine [almost never has red maple, northern red oak, or basswood]. Most often on outwash plain; occasionally on sandy moraine. Soils typically well-sorted, excessively or somewhat excessively drained sand.
leads.rt: If b + b' < 0....FDn12 Northern Dry-Sand Pine Woodland p. 103

leads.text: Dry-mesic or mesic woodland or forest. Canopy of red pine, white pine, and paper birch, usually mixed with other hardwoods. Most often on moraine or outwash plain. Soils typically well-drained to somewhat excessively well-drained banded sand or poorly sorted outwash sand.
leads.rt: If b + b' ≥ 0 go to c

leads.text: Dry-mesic pine-hardwood woodland. Canopy of red pine, white pine, jack pine, quaking aspen, paper birch or red maple; often with balsam fir or white spruce. Most often on outwash plain; occasionally on moraine; very rarely on till plain. Soils somewhat excessively drained to well-drained sand. Common in MDL.
leads.rt: If c + c' < 0....FDn33 Northern Dry-Mesic Mixed Woodland p. 112

leads.text: Mesic white pine forest, often with red pine, paper birch, or quaking aspen [almost never has jack pine or red oak]. Most often on till plain or moraine; occasionally on outwash plain. Well-drained coarse-loamy soils. Documented only in northeastern portion of MDL.
leads.rt: If c + c' ≥ 0....FDn43 Northern Mesic Mixed Forest p. 115

leads.text: Central Floristic (FDc) Region species present (Table FD-2, p. 100). Canopy dominated by jack pine or red pine with white pine, quaking aspen, and paper birch [almost never has balsam fir or white spruce]. Usually on outwash plain or moraine; rarely on sand dune. On excessively drained to well-drained sandy soils, occasionally with darkened surface horizons from former prairie vegetation. Most common in the southwestern half of MDL.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≥ 0 go to d

leads.text: Dry jack pine woodland, often with scattered hardwoods. Canopy dominated by jack pine, occasionally with red pine [almost never has white pine or red maple]. Low-shrubs, especially blueberries, commonly have >5% cover. Ground layer often has more than five graminoid species. On deep well-sorted sand associated with outwash plain or sandy lacustrine deposit.
leads.rt: If d + d' < 0 go to e

leads.text: Poor dry jack pine woodland. Understory open. Low-shrubs, especially blueberries, commonly have >25% cover. Ground layer mossy. Often on very well-sorted lacustrine sand; occasionally on outwash plain.
leads.rt: If e + e' < 0....FDc12 Central Poor Dry Pine Woodland p. 118

leads.text: Dry jack pine woodland usually with scattered hardwoods. Canopy nearly closed. Tall-shrubs often abundant; low-shrubs have <25% cover. Ground layer with scattered patches of mosses. Usually on outwash plain; rarely on lacustrine sand.
leads.rt: If e + e' ≥ 0....FDc23 Central Dry Pine Woodland p.120

leads.text: Dry or dry-mesic pine or pine-hardwood woodland or forest. Canopy is a mixture of jack pine, red pine, and hardwoods. Low-shrub cover rarely >5%. Ground layer rarely has more than five graminoid species. On sandy or gravelly soils; most often on outwash plain with banded deposits or on partially supraglacial drift on sorted moraine.
leads.rt: If d + d' ≥ 0 go to f

leads.text: Dry jack pine woodland. [Canopy almost never has white pine, red maple, big-toothed aspen, or basswood]. Usually on outwash plain; very rarely on moraine or till plain. On excessively well-drained to well-drained sand with horizons differing mostly by color.
leads.rt: If f + f' ≤ 0....FDc24 Central Rich Dry Pine Woodland p. 122

leads.text: Dry-mesic pine, pine-hardwood, or hardwood forest. Canopy of red pine, white pine, or paper birch. Most often on moraine; occasionally on till plain; rarely on outwash plain. On well-drained to somewhat excessively drained sandy and gravelly soils with subsoil horizons that can perch water.
leads.rt: If f + f' > 0....FDc34 Central Dry-Mesic Pine-Hardwood Forest p. 127

leads.text: Dry-mesic to wet-mesic forest. Northern Floristic (MHn) Region species present (Table MH-1, p. 134). Canopy of sugar maple, basswood, and paper birch OR dominated by quaking aspen [almost never has black cherry or hackberry]. Ferns and fern allies often present in ground layer. Most often on moraine with outwash or till plain inclusions. On well-drained to somewhat poorly drained soils with subsoil horizons that hold water.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≤ 0 go to b

leads.text: Mesic or dry-mesic hardwood forest, sometimes mixed with conifers. Canopy of sugar maple, basswood, paper birch, or northern red oak [almost never has black ash, balsam poplar or black spruce]. On well-drained to moderately well-drained, fine-loamy soils.
leads.rt: If b + b' < 0 go to c

leads.text: Mesic to dry-mesic hardwood forest, occasionally mixed with conifers. Canopy of sugar maple, basswood, and paper birch [almost never has white cedar or black ash]. Most often on moraine; occasionally on till plain. On well-drained to moderately well-drained, fine-textured soils; rarely with silt cap.
leads.rt: If c + c' ≤ 0....MHn35 Northern Mesic Hardwood Forest p. 136

leads.text: Mesic hardwood forest, rarely mixed with conifers. Canopy of sugar maple, basswood, and yellow birch [almost never has red maple, big-toothed aspen, bur oak, white spruce, white pine, or red pine]. Most often on till plain, occasionally on moraine. On well-drained to moderately well-drained, fine-textured soils; commonly with silt cap.
leads.rt: If c + c' > 0....MHn47 Northern Rich Mesic Hardwood Forest p. 147

leads.text: Wet-mesic hardwood forest, commonly mixed with conifers. Canopy dominated by quaking aspen, paper birch, black ash, red maple,or basswood [almost never has sugar maple or ironwood]. On moderately well-drained to somewhat poorly drained, coarse-loamy to sandy soils.
leads.rt: If b + b' ≥ 0 go to d

leads.text: Wet-mesic hardwood or hardwood-conifer forest, usually with evidence of conifer dominance in the past. Canopy dominated by quaking aspen, paper birch, and red maple. Most often on coarse-loamy moraine with outwash inclusions; occasionally on lake-washed till plain. On well-drained to somewhat poorly drained soils.
leads.rt: If d + d' ≤ 0....MHn44 No. Wet-Mesic Boreal Hardwood-Conifer Forest p. 139

leads.text: Wet-mesic hardwood forest, rarely with conifers. Canopy dominated by black ash, basswood, and quaking aspen [almost never has balsam fir or white spruce]. Most often on fine-loamy till plain; occasionally on moraine. On moderately well-drained to poorly drained soils.
leads.rt: If d + d' > 0....MHn46 Northern Wet-Mesic Hardwood Forest p. 144

leads.text: Dry-mesic or mesic forest. Central Floristic (MHc) Region species present (Table MH-2, p. 134). Canopy of northern red oak, paper birch, sugar maple or basswood [almost never has balsam fir, yellow birch, black ash, white spruce or white cedar]. Fern allies seldom present in ground layer. Most often on hummocky moraine with inclusions of outwash; rarely on till plain. On somewhat excessively drained to moderately well-drained soils with subsoil horizons that hold water; occasionally on sandy soils that hold water because of dense texture or complex textural banding.
leads.rt: If a + a' > 0 go to e

leads.text: Dry-mesic hardwood forest, occasionally mixed with pine. Canopy of northern red oak, paper birch, quaking aspen, bur oak, or red maple; often with sugar maple, basswood, big-toothed aspen, red pine, or white pine [almost never has American elm or green ash]. On well-drained to moderately well-drained soils with abrupt transition between thin topsoil layer and light-colored horizons below. Widespread in MDL.

leads.text: Mesic hardwood forest, very rarely with pine. Canopy dominated by sugar maple and basswood; often mixed with northern red oak and lesser amounts of paper birch, quaking aspen, bur oak, or ironwood [almost never has red maple, big-toothed aspen, red pine or white pine]. On well-drained or moderately well-drained soils with dark-colored surface horizons. Uncommon to rare in MDL.
leads.rt: If e + e' ≥ 0 go to f

leads.text: Canopy of northern red oak, paper birch, quaking aspen, bur oak, and red maple. On well-drained or moderately well-drained soils with subsoil horizons that can perch water. Rare in MDL, probably limited to fire-protected sites on islands or peninsulas.
leads.rt: If f + f' < 0....MHc36 Central Mesic Hardwood Forest (Eastern) p. 153

leads.text: Canopy dominated by sugar maple and basswood [almost never has red maple, big-toothed aspen, red pine or white pine]. On well-drained relict prairie soils with thick, dark topsoil layer grading to lighter horizons below. Documented in MDL only in Itasca State Park; likely in nearby areas.
leads.rt: If f + f' ≥ 0....MHc37 Central Mesic Hardwood Forest (Western) p. 156

leads.text: Wet riparian hardwood forest. Canopy dominated by black ash and silver maple, often with some green ash, basswood, bur oak, or American elm. Most often on rarely to occasionally flooded alluvial or cut terrace along medium or large river. On moderately well-drained to poorly drained silty or, occasionally, sandy soils.

leads.text: Very wet riparian hardwood forest. Canopy dominated by silver maple with some American elm, green ash, or black ash [bur oak and basswood are absent or have low abundance]. Most often on annually flooded alluvial plain. On poorly drained sandy soils subject to scouring and deposition from floodwater.

leads.text: Wet conifer or conifer-hardwood forest. Canopy dominated by white cedar, sometimes with abundant black ash [almost never has red elm, red maple or American elm]. Feathermosses often important in ground layer.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≤ 0 ....WFn53 Northern Wet Cedar Forest p. 177

leads.text: Wet or very wet hardwood forest, often mixed with some conifers. Canopy dominated by black ash, often mixed with lesser amounts of white cedar, balsam poplar, quaking aspen, or paper birch. Ground layer with sparse cover of dark-green, thin-leaved mosses (Plagiomnium).

leads.text: Wet hardwood forest, usually with some scattered conifers. Canopy typically closed, with crowns touching or overlapping. Dominated by black ash, occasionally mixed with other hardwood species, especially yellow birch, paper birch, or quaking aspen. Most often in drain or transition between wetland and upland. Often with small streams and rivulets or moving surface water.

Most often in closed depression or very flat area. Rarely with streams or moving surface water.

leads.text: Dry to mesic hardwood-conifer or conifer woodland or forest. Northern Floristic (FDn) Region species present (Table FD-1, p. 99). Canopy of red pine, red maple, paper birch or white pine [almost never has jack pine, northern pin oak or bur oak]. Fern allies often present in ground layer. Most commonly on till plain with very stony, shallow till over bedrock; occasionally on coarse-textured drift where erosion has concentrated stones or deposited sand on the soil surface. On excessively to well-drained soils mostly lacking diagnostic horizons but commonly with some development of a whitish horizon beneath the duff.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≤ 0 go to b

leads.text: Dry pine woodland occasionally mixed with hardwoods. Canopy dominated by red pine with white pine and big-toothed aspen [almost never has balsam fir or white spruce]. Most commonly in abandoned channel of St. Louis or Kettle River characterized by shallow, very stony drift and bedrock outcrops. On excessively drained shallow soils lacking diagnostic horizons.
leads.rt: If b + b' < 0 ....FDn22 Northern Dry-Bedrock Pine (Oak) Woodland p. 106

leads.text: Mesic hardwood-conifer or hardwood forest. Canopy of paper birch, quaking aspen, red maple, and balsam fir; typically with large red and white pine stumps or with scattered old pines. Most commonly on stony till of Split Rock & Nickerson phases of Superior Lobe. On somewhat excessively to well-drained stony soils with sandy surface often over finer-textured material.
leads.rt: If b + b' ≥ 0 ....FDn43 Northern Mesic Mixed Forest p. 115

leads.text: Dry or dry-mesic woodland or forest. Central Floristic (FDc) Region species present (Table FD-2, p. 100). Canopy dominated by jack pine or mixed with northern pin oak or quaking aspen [almost never has balsam fir or white spruce]. Fern allies seldom present in ground layer. Almost always on sandy terrace in or near St. Croix River Valley; occasionally on sandy outwash of Rainy or Superior lobe. On excessively to somewhat excessively drained deep sandy soils with horizons differentiated by color; whitish horizon often present beneath duff.
leads.rt: If a + a' > 0 go to c

leads.text: Dry pine woodland. Canopy strongly dominated by jack pine with northern red oak or bur oak [almost never has quaking aspen, northern pin oak, big-toothed aspen, paper birch or red maple].
leads.rt: If c + c' < 0 ....FDc23 Central Dry Pine Woodland p. 120

leads.text: Dry or dry-mesic woodland or forest. Canopy dominated by jack pine or mixed with quaking aspen, big-toothed aspen, and northern pin oak.
leads.rt: If c + c' ≥ 0 go to d

leads.text: Dry or dry-mesic woodland or forest. Canopy variable. Most commonly present on outwash plains northwest of WSU, especially in Crow Wing County; rare in WSU.
leads.rt: If d + d' ≤ 0 go to e

leads.text: Dry pine or hardwood-pine woodland. Canopy dominated by jack pine mixed with red pine [almost never has white pine, red maple, big-toothed aspen, or basswood]. Most commonly on outwash plain; very rarely on moraine or till plain. On sandy soils with horizons differing mostly by color. Rare in WSU.
leads.rt: If e + e' < 0 ....FDc24 Central Rich Dry Pine Woodland p. 122

leads.text: Dry-mesic forest. Canopy of red pine, white pine, quaking aspen, or paper birch. Most commonly on moraine; occasionally on till; rarely on outwash plain. On sandy or gravelly soils with subsoil horizons that can perch water. Rare in WSU.
leads.rt: If e + e' ≥ 0 ....FDc34 Central Dry-Mesic Pine-Hardwood Forest p. 127

leads.text: Dry hardwood or hardwood-pine woodland. Canopy dominated by northern pin oak, quaking aspen, or jack pine. Usually on sandy outwash or abandoned terrace along St. Croix River or Kettle River.
leads.rt: If d + d' > 0 ....FDc25 Central Dry Oak-Aspen (Pine) Woodland p. 125

leads.text: Dry-mesic to wet-mesic hardwood or hardwood-conifer forest. Northern Floristic (MHn) Region species present (Table MH-1, p. 134). Canopy of sugar maple, paper birch, basswood, or quaking aspen [almost never has bitternut hickory, white oak, butternut, white ash, American elm, red elm, northern pin oak, black cherry, or blue beech]. Ferns and fern allies often present in ground layer. Usually on lake plain, till plain, or moraine. On well-drained to somewhat poorly drained soils with subsoil horizons that hold water.
leads.rt: If a + a' < 0 go to b

leads.text: Mesic hardwood forest, rarely mixed with conifers but may have had white pine historically. Canopy dominated by sugar maple with basswood, paper birch, or northern red oak [almost never has bur oak, balsam poplar, white cedar, American elm or red elm]. Usually on moraine or till plain of the Superior Lobe; occasionally on lake plain of Glacial Lake Duluth. On well to moderately well-drained soils with dense subsoil horizons that perch water.
leads.rt: If b + b' < 0 go to c

leads.text: Mesic or dry-mesic hardwood forest, rarely mixed with conifers. Canopy of sugar maple, basswood, paper birch, northern red oak, or red maple [almost never has white pine, black ash or green ash]. Most commonly on moraine or till plain of the Superior Lobe; occasionally on dissected lake plain of Glacial Lake Duluth. Present on slope of any aspect. On well-drained, sandy-loam soils with dense, firm, partially cemented subsoil horizons that perch water.
leads.rt: If c + c' ≤ 0 ....MHn35 Northern Mesic Hardwood Forest p. 136

leads.text: Rich mesic hardwood forest, occasionally mixed with conifers or probably had white pine historically. Canopy dominated by sugar maple with basswood, yellow birch and paper birch. Most commonly on dissected lake plain of Glacial Lake Duluth or Glacial Lake Upham; occasionally on Superior Lobe moraine or till plain. Typically on N- to E-facing slope. On moderately well- or somewhat poorly drained, fine-loamy soils; subsoil horizons have firm consistency and fine texture (rarely cemented) and can perch water.
leads.rt: If c + c' > 0 ....MHn47 Northern Rich Mesic Hardwood Forest p. 147

leads.text: Wet-mesic or mesic forest. Canopy of quaking aspen, paper birch, red maple, black ash, white spruce, or white pine [almost never has ironwood and big-toothed aspen]. Most commonly on dissected lake plain of Glacial Lake Duluth or level Superior Lobe till plain; very rarely on moraine. On well-drained to moderately well-drained soils with subsoil horizons that perch water because of fine texture and firm consistency.
leads.rt: If b + b' ≥ 0 go to d

leads.text: Wet-mesic or mesic forest with conifers present or with stumps, down logs, or other evidence of former importance of conifers. Canopy of quaking aspen, paper birch, white spruce, and red maple [almost never has black ash, sugar maple, bur oak, yellow birch or big-toothed aspen]. Most commonly on lake plain, especially sandy shoreline deposit or sandy bottom within dissected Glacial Lake Duluth Plain; occasionally on moraine or till plain. On somewhat poorly drained, coarse-loamy soils; occasionally on well-drained or moderately well-drained sandy soils in wet landscapes.
leads.rt: If d + d' < 0 ....MHn44 No. Wet-Mesic Boreal Hardwood-Conifer Forest p. 139

leads.text: Wet-mesic lowland hardwood forest typically without conifers; if conifers are present they have low abundance. Canopy of black ash, quaking aspen, basswood, sugar maple, or bur oak [almost never has white pine, balsam fir, or red pine]. Most commonly on Superior Lobe till plain; occasionally on clayey flat of Glacial Lake Duluth Plain or on moraine. On somewhat poorly drained or moderately well-drained fine-loamy soils.
leads.rt: If d + d' ≥ 0 ....MHn46 Northern Wet-Mesic Hardwood Forest p. 144

leads.text: Dry-mesic to wet-mesic hardwood forest rarely mixed with conifers. Central Floristic (MHc) Region species present (Table MH-2, p. 134). Canopy of northern red oak, basswood, sugar maple, red maple, or green ash [almost never has white spruce, yellow birch, balsam fir, white cedar or balsam poplar]. Ferns and fern allies seldom present in ground layer. Most commonly on moraine or till plain; not usually present on lake plain. On somewhat excessively to moderately well-drained soils.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≥ 0 go to e

leads.text: Dry-mesic or mesic hardwood forest. Canopy dominated by northern red oak and basswood. Forb cover usually <75% and graminoid cover usually <5%. Most often on gravelly moraine or associated outwash of the Superior Lobe; occasionally on Superior Lobe till plain. On somewhat excessively drained to moderately well-drained soils.
leads.rt: If e + e' ≤ 0 go to f

leads.text: Dry-mesic hardwood forest formerly with red and white pine; pine stumps and evidence of past surface fires such as charcoal and fire-scarred trees are often present. Canopy typically dominated by northern red oak with paper birch, red maple, basswood, and quaking aspen [almost never has black ash]. On somewhat excessively drained or well-drained sandy or gravelly soils with subsoil horizons capable of perching water discontinuous and local.

sp.s: Rubus allegheniensis and similar Rubus spp.

leads.rt: If f + f' < 0 ....MHc26 Central Dry-Mesic Oak-Aspen Forest p. 150

leads.text: Mesic hardwood forest, very rarely with pine stumps or evidence of natural fires. Canopy of basswood, northern red oak, and sugar maple with green ash and paper birch [almost never has red or white pine]. On mostly well-drained or moderately well-drained soils with subsoil horizons that can perch water.
leads.rt: If f + f' ≥ 0 ....MHc36 Central Mesic Hardwood Forest (Eastern) p. 153

leads.text: Wet-mesic hardwood forest. Canopy of basswood, black ash, bur oak, sugar maple, green ash, or northern red oak [almost never has white oak, bitternut hickory or white ash]. Forb cover usually >75% and graminoid cover usually >5%. Usually on sandy outwash or terrace along the St. Croix River; commonly also on coarse-loamy Superior Lobe (St. Croix Phase) till. On somewhat poorly drained soils or occasionally on moderately well-drained, sandy soils in glacial drain or abandoned terrace.
leads.rt: If e + e' > 0 ....MHc47 Central Wet-Mesic Hardwood Forest p. 158

leads.text: Wet riparian hardwood forest. Canopy of black ash, basswood, silver maple, bur oak, or green ash. Shrub-layer cover typically >25%. Cover of ferns and fern allies relatively high (>25%), usually with two or more species present. Most often on terrace that is rarely flooded; evidence of recent flooding generally lacking.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≤ 0 ....FFn57 Northern Terrace Forest p. 164

leads.text: Very wet riparian hardwood forest. Canopy strongly dominated by silver maple with scattered individuals of other tree species. Shrub layer usually absent or with <25% cover. Cover of ferns and fern allies relatively low (often <5%), usually with only one species present. Dense cover of ostrich ferns may be present in swales. Most often on floodplain that is flooded annually; ice-scars, piles of woody debris, active levees, or meander scrolls typically present.
leads.rt: If a + a' > 0 ....FFn67 Northern Floodplain Forest p. 166

leads.text: Wet or very wet conifer, hardwood-conifer, or hardwood forest. Northern Floristic (WFn) Region species present (Table WF-1, p. 172). Canopy dominated either by white cedar, often mixed with black ash and other conifers; OR by black ash or red maple mixed with yellow birch and other conifers. Most often in depression in flat landscape; occasionally at toe of slope, with slight evidence of groundwater seepage; surface water is near air temperature or cool, but not cold.
leads.rt: If a + a' < 0 go to b

leads.text: Wet white cedar forest, often with some hardwoods. Canopy dominated by white cedar usually mixed with lesser amounts of balsam fir, black ash, or white pine. Typically, two or more conifer species are present.
leads.rt: If b + b' < 0 ....WFn53 Northern Wet Cedar Forest p. 177

leads.text: Wet or very wet hardwood forest mixed with some conifers. Canopy dominated by black ash or red maple [almost never has white cedar]. Typically, no more than one conifer species present.
leads.rt: If b + b' ≥ 0 go to c

leads.text: Wet hardwood forest, occasionally with a few conifers. Canopy of black ash, yellow birch, or red maple with other hardwoods [almost never has tamarack]. Typically with <50% cover of grasses and sedges.
leads.rt: If c + c' < 0 ....WFn55 Northern Wet Ash Swamp p. 180

leads.text: Very wet hardwood forest, occasionally with a few conifers. Canopy strongly dominated by black ash, occasionally with yellow birch, red maple, paper birch, or tamarack [almost never has white spruce or white pine]. Typically with >50% cover of grasses and sedges.
leads.rt: If c + c' ≥ 0 ....WFn64 Northern Very Wet Ash Swamp p. 183

leads.text: Wet hardwood forest, very rarely with conifers. Southern Floristic (WFs) Region species present (Table WF-2, p. 173). Canopy dominated by black ash, often mixed with basswood and yellow birch [almost never has white cedar, balsam fir, white pine, paper birch, white spruce, tamarack, or black spruce]. Often at toe of high, steep slope; groundwater seepage obvious. If flowing springs are present, water is noticeably cold.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≥ 0 ....WFs57 Southern Wet Ash Swamp p. 186

leads.text: Conifer or shrub swamp present throughout WSU. Dominated by tamarack or tall shrubs, typically speckled alder; black spruce may be present. Northern Floristic (FPn) Region species are present (Table FP-1 p. 193).
leads.rt: If a + a' < 0 go to b

leads.text: Conifer swamp, tree cover >25 %. Dominated by tamarack.
leads.rt: If b + b' < 0 ....FPn72 Northern Rich Tamarack Swamp (Eastern Basin) p. 203

leads.text: Shrub swamp dominated by speckled alder, typically with >75% cover. Trees absent or with <25% cover.
leads.rt: If b + b' ≥ 0 ....FPn73 Northern Alder Swamp p. 205

leads.text: Conifer swamp of Eastern Broadleaf Province, with range extending onto Grantsburg Sublobe in southern part of WSU. Southern Floristic (FPs) Region species are present (Table FP-1, p. 193). Dominated by tamarack; black spruce absent.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≥ 0 ....FPs63 Southern Rich Conifer Swamp p. 211

leads.text: Wooded peatland; trees taller than 16ft (5m) have >25% cover. Sites burned in past may lack tree canopy but shade-tolerant understory species persist for decades.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≤ 0 go to b

leads.text: Only bog species are present (see Appendix D). Minerotrophic species, if present, are restricted to tree seedlings and are short lived.
leads.rt: If b + b' = 0 ....APn80 Northern Spruce Bog p. 219

leads.text: Both minerotrophic and bog species are present.
leads.rt: If b + b' > 0 ....APn81 Northern Poor Conifer Swamp p. 222

leads.text: Open to sparsely wooded peatland; trees taller than 16ft (5m) usually have <25% cover.
leads.rt: If a + a' > 0 go to c

leads.text: Only bog species are present (See Appendix D).
leads.rt: If c + c' = 0 ....APn90 Northern Open Bog p. 225

leads.text: Both minerotrophic and bog species are present.
leads.rt: If c + c' > 0 ....APn91 Northern Poor Fen p. 228

leads.text: Substrate composed of boulders and rock fragments (talus) eroded from upslope cliff or rock outcrop. Generally on steep slope. Very rare (if present at all) in WSU/SSU.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≤ 0 ....CTn12 Northern Open Talus p. 236

leads.text: Substrate composed of vertical or nearly vertical bedrock exposure (cliff), generally greater than 6ft (2m) tall.
leads.rt: If a + a' > 0 go to b

leads.text: Dry cliff, generally with southeast to west aspect and majority of cliff exposed to direct sunlight. Vascular plants, mosses, and algae sparse. Crustose lichens are dominant cover. Trees rare on cliff face. Present occasionally along St. Louis, Kettle, and St. Croix Rivers.
leads.rt: If b + b' ≤ 0 ....CTn11 Northern Dry Cliff p. 234

leads.text: Dry-mesic to wet cliff, generally with northwest to east aspect and majority of cliff face shaded by tree canopy or because of aspect or setting. Mosses, lichens, and algae have moderate to dense cover. Vascular plants, including woody species, have sparse to moderate cover. Trees usually present on cliff face and often deformed.
leads.rt: If b + b' > 0 go to c

leads.text: Dry-mesic to mesic cliff with groundwater seepage absent or generally evident on <1/3 of cliff face. Vascular plants common though largely restricted to crevices and ledges. Mosses, lichens, and algae common, with lichens having the greatest cover. Present along St. Louis and Kettle Rivers; rare in WSU/SSU.
leads.rt: If c + c' < 0 ....CTn32 Northern Mesic Cliff p. 240

leads.text: Wet-mesic to wet cliff with groundwater seepage generally evident on >1/3 of face. Vascular plants common on crevices and ledges as well as on moss mats. Mosses, lichens, and algae common, with mosses and algae having the greatest cover; thick moss mats cover large portions of cliff face. Present along the Kettle River; very rare in WSU/SSU.
leads.rt: If c + c' ≥ 0 ....CTn42 Northern Wet Cliff p. 243

leads.text: Open dry communities on exposed bedrock. Shrub and tree cover sparse or absent. Crustose lichens are predominant cover, with foliose species common. Deeper soil surrounding bedrock exposures supports woodland or forest. Generally small communities (<5ac (<2ha)) in openings in woodlands or forests on ridge tops, slopes, or exposed horizontal or sloping bedrock above cliffs. Uncommon but occurring at a number of places in WSU/SSU.
leads.rt: ROn12 Northern Bedrock Outcrop p. 251

leads.text: Shrub-dominated dry to dry-mesic communities on matrix of exposed bedrock and deeper soil. Lichens dominant on exposed bedrock. Woody plants dominant in deeper soil, generally with 25-75% cover overall. Scattered small, open-grown trees common. Evidence of fire often present. Small to medium-sized communities (1 to >25ac (0.4 to >10ha)) on ridge tops, slopes, or exposed horizontal or sloping bedrock above cliffs. Very rare (if present at all) in WSU/SSU.
leads.rt: ROn23 Northern Bedrock Shrubland p. 253

leads.text: Substrate composed of pieces of fractured bedrock and cobbles <3ft (1m) long, or finer material such as gravel, sand, silt, or clay. Present along lakeshores across Minnesota.
leads.rt: If a + a' < 0 go to b

leads.text: Substrate composed of sand, gravel, or cobbles.
leads.rt: If b + b' < 0 ....LKi32 Inland Lake Sand/Gravel/Cobble Shore p. 259

leads.text: Substrate composed of silt or clay.
leads.rt: If b + b' ≥ 0 ....LKi54 Inland Lake Clay/Mud Shore p. 263

leads.text: Substrate composed of solid rock or large pieces of rock, including bedrock outcrops, large pieces of fractured bedrock, or large glacial erratics >3ft (1m) long. Very rare (if present at all) in WSU/SSU.
leads.rt: If a + a' = 0 ....LKi43 Inland Lake Rocky Shore p. 261

leads.text: Sparsely vegetated river shore, sand bar, or intermittent streambed with primary substrate of sand, gravel, cobbles, boulders, or bedrock.

leads.rt: RVx32 Sand/Gravel/Cobble River Shore p. 270

leads.text: River shore or intermittent streambed with substrate of bedrock or boulders >3ft (1m) long.
leads.rt: RVx43 Rocky River Shore p. 272

leads.text: Sparsely vegetated river beach, mud flat, or steep slumping riverbank with substrate of silt or clay.
leads.rt: If a + a' = 0 ....RVx54 Clay/Mud River Shore p. 274

leads.text: Shrubby peatland dominated by leatherleaf, bog birch, or sweet gale with graminoid layer dominated by broad-leaved sedges and grasses (e.g., bluejoint [Calamagrostis canadensis], lake sedge [Carex lacustris]). Often associated with peatland bordering lake or river shore or in lagg between peatland and upland. Periodically exposed to surface flooding.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≤ 0 ....OPn81 Northern Shrub Shore Fen p. 281

leads.text: Graminoid or shrubby peatland; shrubs, if present, typically dominated by willows; graminoids dominated by fine-leaved species (e.g., fen wiregrass sedge, creeping sedge [Carex chordorrhiza]). Present in basin or on floating mat adjacent to lake or river. Not exposed to surface flooding.
leads.rt: If a + a' > 0 ....OPn92 Northern Rich Fen (Basin) p. 286
WMn82 Northern Wet Meadow/Carr p. 292

leads.text: Emergent marsh dominated by cattails (Typha spp.), usually with >50% cover. Sedges commonly present. Substrate is mineral soil or peat. Often present on floating mat. Associated with sheltered to moderately wave-washed shore.
leads.rt: MRn83 Northern Mixed Cattail Marsh p. 298

leads.text: Emergent marsh dominated by bulrushes or spikerushes (e.g., soft stem bulrush [Scirpus validus], river bulrush [S. fluviatilis], hardstem bulrush [S. acutus], slender bulrush [S. heterochaetus], and Small's spikerush [Eleocharis smallii]). Substrate is mineral soil. Associated with wave-washed shore.
leads.rt: MRn93 Northern Bulrush-Spikerush Marsh p. 299
FDs36 Southern Dry-Mesic Oak-Aspen Forest p. 75
MHs38 Southern Mesic Oak-Basswood Forest p. 111

leads.text: Wet riparian hardwood forest. Canopy of basswood, box elder, American elm, and green ash; sometimes with black ash, quaking aspen, and balsam poplar. Most often on stream or river terrace, rarely flooded or flooded for short duration; evidence of recent flooding generally absent.
leads.rt: FFn57 Northern Terrace Forest p. 137

leads.text: Very wet riparian hardwood forest. Canopy of green ash, American elm, box elder, black willow, or cottonwood [never or rarely with basswood, black ash, balsam poplar, or quaking aspen]. Most often on river floodplain, flooded annually for long duration; ice-scars, piles of woody debris, active levees, and meander scrolls typically present.
leads.rt: FFn67 Northern Floodplain Forest p. 141

leads.text: Sparsely to densely vegetated lakeshore on substrate composed of sand, gravel, or cobbles.
leads.rt: LKi32 Inland Lake Sand/Gravel/Cobble Shore p. 209

leads.text: Sparsely to densely vegetated lakeshore on substrate composed of silt or clay.
leads.rt: LKi54 Inland Lake Clay/Mud Shore p. 209

leads.text: Sparsely to densely vegetated river shore, gravel bar, sand bar, or intermittent streambed with substrate of sand, gravel, or cobbles.
leads.rt: RVx32 Sand/Gravel/Cobble River Shore p. 212

leads.text: Sparsely to densely vegetated river shore, mud flat, or steep slumping riverbank with substrate of silt or clay.
leads.rt: RVx54 Clay/Mud River Shore p. 213

leads.text: Species-rich or somewhat species-poor grassland or savanna dominated by a combination of tall, midheight, and short grasses, including big bluestem (Andropogon gerardii), little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium), porcupine grass (Stipa spartea), and blue grama (Bouteloua gracilis). Junegrass (Koeleria pyramidata), needle-and-thread (Stipa comata), prairie dropseed (Sporobolus heterolepis), and side-oats grama (Bouteloua curtipendula) are other major grasses. Bare or lichen-encrusted soil surface often visible. Present on a variety of landforms where moisture availability is sharply limited by some combination of substrate and steep slopes. Soils are somewhat excessively to excessively drained, mostly coarse-textured sandy loams and loamy sands, often with a substantial gravel fraction; also aeolian sand deposits. The dark-colored surface layer is generally <9in (23cm) thick, but absent in dune sands.
leads.rt: If a + a' < 0 go to b

leads.text: Trees >6ft (2m) tall rare or absent (cover <10%); woody plants mostly leadplant (Amorpha canescens) and prairie rose (Rosa arkansana); sage wormwood (Artemisia frigida) is also frequent.
leads.rt: UPn12 Northern Dry Prairie p. 220

leads.text: Trees >6ft (2m) tall present as scattered individuals or as scattered small clumps (total cover >10%). Bur oak is the principal species, but northern pin oak may also be present. Shrubs (including oak “grubs” up to 6ft tall) sparse to common (cover 5-50%). The most frequent shrubs in addition to species listed above for UPn12 are wolfberry (Symphoricarpos occidentalis), sand cherry (Prunus pumila), and chokecherry (Prunus virginiana).
leads.rt: UPn13 Northern Dry Savanna p. 225

leads.text: Species-rich grassland or savanna dominated by tall grasses big bluestem and Indian grass (Sorghastrum nutans), with tall and midheight grasses little bluestem, prairie dropseed, porcupine grass, and switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) also important; some wet prairie species such as prairie cordgrass (Spartina pectinata) and mat muhly grass (Muhlenbergia richardsonis) often present, but less abundant. Soil surface typically completely obscured by vegetation. On nearly level to moderately rolling landforms. Soils are deep, loamy, moderately well drained and well drained, and have a dark-colored surface horizon that is usually ≥9in (23cm) thick.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≥ 0 go to c

leads.text: Trees >6ft (2m) tall rare or absent (cover <10%); woody plants mostly leadplant and prairie rose.
leads.rt: UPn23 Northern Mesic Prairie p. 231

leads.text: Trees >6ft (2m) tall (principally bur oak) present as scattered individuals or as scattered small clumps (total cover >10%). Shrubs (may include oak “grubs” up to 6ft tall) usually common (cover 25-75%). The most frequent shrubs in addition to species listed above for UPn23 include wolfberry, chokecherry, American hazelnut (Corylus americana), Saskatoon juneberry (Amelanchier alnifolia), and gray dogwood (Cornus racemosa).
leads.rt: UPn24 Northern Mesic Savanna p. 236

leads.text: Open peatland dominated by fen wiregrass sedge (Carex lasiocarpa). Wetland Prairie species uncommon. Pools with marl or tufa deposits absent.
leads.rt: If a + a' ≤ 0 ....OPp91 Prairie Rich Fen p. 265

leads.text: Open peatland with areas dominated by sterile sedge (Carex sterilis) or hair-like beak rush (Rhynchospora capillacea) almost always present. Wetland Prairie species (including big bluestem [Andropogon gerardii], mat muhly grass [Muhlenbergia richardsonis], Riddell's goldenrod [Solidago riddellii], and other species) are usually present. Pools with marl or tufa deposits typically present.
leads.rt: If a + a' > 0 ....OPp93 Prairie Extremely Rich Fen p. 270

leads.text: Open, graminoid- or shrub-dominated wetland. Northern Floristic (WMn) Region species present (Table WM-1, p. 277). Dominant graminoid typically lake sedge (Carex lacustris) or aquatic sedge (C. aquatilis). Uncommon in RRV.

leads.text: Open, graminoid- or shrub-dominated wetland. Southern Floristic (WMs) or Prairie Floristic (WMp) Region species present (Table WM-1 p. 278). Dominant graminoid typically species other than lake sedge (Carex lacustris). Common in RRV.

sp.s: Helianthus giganteus, H. grosseserratus, or H. nuttallii

leads.text: Open, graminoid- or shrub-dominated wetland. Southern Floristic (WMs) Region species present (Table WM-1, p. 278). Dominant graminoid typically tussock sedge (Carex stricta), beaked sedge (C. utriculata), slough sedge (C. atherodes), aquatic sedge (C. aquatilis), narrow reedgrass (Calamagrostis stricta), or whitetop (Scolochloa festucacea).
leads.rt: If b + b' < 0 go to c

leads.text: Dominated by graminoids or shrubs. Dominant graminoid typically tussock sedge (Carex stricta) or aquatic sedge (C. aquatilis). Usually associated with groundwater seepage area at base of river terrace or on gentle slope. Can also occur in level wetland dissected by stream or river.

sp.s: Helianthus giganteus, H. grosseserratus, or H. nuttallii

APn80.intro: Only one plant community type is recognized in this class. It is divided into two subtypes along a continuum from well-developed to sparse tree canopies.

units.name: Treed Subtype
units.text: Canopy is variable but typically has >50% cover of black spruce. Tree cover is sufficient to provide conditions for a relatively high number and cover of shade-tolerant species, including lingonberry (Vaccinium vitis-idaea), Indian pipe (Monotropa uniflora), velvet-leaved blueberry (V. myrtilloides), and lowbush blueberry (V. angustifolium). APn80a1 is best developed on upper portions of raised bog crests, where drainage is more suitable for tree growth than in APn80a2. Description is based on summary of vegetation data from 28 plots.

cov.text: typically has >50% cover of black spruce

site: upper portions of raised bog crests
drainage is more suitable for tree growth than in APn80a2

units.name: Semi-Treed Subtype
units.text: Canopy is relatively open because of water tables high enough to limit tree development. Canopy trees are stunted and patchy, with <50% cover. Species with greater light requirements are more common and more abundant in APn80a2 than in APn80a1, including tamarack, few-fruited sedge (Carex pauciflora), pitcher plant (Sarracenia purpurea), and tussock cottongrass (Eriophorum vaginatum). APn80a2 occurs in incipient bog drains and at the bases of bog crests. Description is based on summary of vegetation data from 46 plots.

units.name: Poor Black Spruce Swamp
units.text: Tree canopy has > 50% cover, typically dominated by black spruce, occasionally with tamarack (which rarely may be codominant). Paper birch is also occasionally present in the canopy. Tall shrubs are usually absent or infrequent. APn81a occurs in slightly drier areas than APn81b and as a result has a denser tree canopy and greater presence of shade-tolerant species in the understory, including Indian pipe, creeping snowberry, ferns (especially Dryopteris spp.), lingonberry (Vaccinium vitis-idaea), soft-leaved sedge (Carex disperma), clubmosses and groundpines (Lycopodium spp.), bunchberry (Cornus canadensis), juneberries (Amelanchier spp.), and balsam fir. Description is based on summary of vegetation data from 21 plots.

units.name: Poor Tamarack - Black Spruce Swamp
units.text: Tree canopy has 25–50% cover and is dominated by black spruce with occasional tamarack, or by tamarack with black spruce. APn81b develops in slightly wetter areas than APn81a. Because of this, APn81b has a more open canopy and more light-demanding species in the understory, including bog rosemary, creeping sedge (Carex chordorrhiza), bog birch, bog wiregrass sedge (C. oligosperma), lake sedge (C. lacustris), few-fruited sedge (C. pauciflora), bog willow (Salix pedicellaris), buckbean (Menyanthes trifoliata), and bog laurel (Kalmia polifolia). APn81b is divided into two subtypes, based on differences in the abundance of black spruce and tamarack in the tree canopy.

units.name: Black Spruce Subtype
units.text: Tree canopy is dominated by black spruce, occasionally with some tamarack. Understory species that help to differentiate APn81b1 from APn81b2 are round-leaved sundew (Drosera rotundifolia), few-fruited sedge (Carex pauciflora), and buckbean. Description is based on summary of vegetation data from 13 plots.

units.name: Tamarack Subtype
units.text: Tree canopy is dominated by tamarack, typically with black spruce, and is slightly more open than the canopy of APn81b1. As a result, bog rosemary and leatherleaf are more abundant in the understory of APn81b2. The presence of lowbush blueberry (Vaccinium angustifolium) in the understory also helps to distinguish APn81b2. Description is based on summary of vegetation data from 16 plots.

units.name: Low Shrub Bog
units.text: Open bogs dominated by ericaceous shrubs, including leatherleaf, Labrador tea, bog laurel, and bog rosemary, which usually have >50% cover. Stunted black spruce and tamarack are often present, and high Sphagnum hummocks are obvious. APn90a occurs at the periphery of raised bogs and in openings in forested bogs. APn90a commonly grades into Black Spruce Bog, Semi-Treed Subtype (see APn80a2).

units.name: Graminoid Bog
units.text: Open bogs dominated by graminoids, including bog wiregrass (Carex oligosperma), tussock cottongrass (Eriophorum vaginatum), and few-fruited sedge (Carex pauciflora). Ericaceous shrub cover is <50% and usually <25%. Hollows and Sphagnum carpets are well developed; high hummocks are less obvious. APn90b is almost always associated with large crested raised bogs and with ovoid bog islands in large patterned peatlands, where it forms incipient water tracks characterized by Sphagnum carpets with low hummocks. APn90b usually does not occur in smaller basins because of the absence of wet hollows. APn90b is divided into two subtypes, based on water-table fluctuations and the presence of pools.

units.name: Schlenke Subtype
units.text: Graminoid-dominated bogs characterized by large temporary pools with scheuchzeria (Scheuchzeria palustris), white beak rush (Rhynchospora alba), and horned bladderwort (Utricularia cornuta). APn90b2 appears to be more typical of bogs in maritime areas than in continental areas, although it lacks some of the typical maritime bryophytes. APn90b2 is rare in Minnesota with only three known occurrences, which are associated with raised bogs in large peatlands.

units.name: Low Shrub Poor Fen
units.text: Open peatlands with cover of leatherleaf and bog birch either > 50% or greater than cover of graminoids, although tussock cottongrass (Eriophorum vaginatum) and tawny cotttongrass (E. virginicum) can be abundant in the graminoid layer. Stunted black spruce and tamarack are often present. Sphagnum hummocks are moderately well developed. Indicator species characteristic of wet hollows are absent or rare. APn91a is present in smaller peatland basins, on floating mats adjacent to ponds and lakes, and at margins or in strings in larger peatlands. Description is based on summary of vegetation data from 76 plots.

units.text: Open peatlands with cover of leatherleaf and bog birch either < 50% or less than cover of graminoids. Indicator species characteristic of wet hollows are frequently present, including white beak rush (Rhynchospora alba), scheuchzeria, candle-lantern sedge (C. limosa), and Sphagnum papillosum. APn91b occurs in smaller peatland basins, on floating mats adjacent to ponds and lakes, and at margins of larger peatlands. Description is based on summary of vegetation data from 55 plots.

units.name: Graminoid Poor Fen (Water Track)
units.text: Open peatlands with cover of leatherleaf and bog birch either < 50% or less than cover of graminoids. Dominant graminoids typically include fen wiregrass sedge (Carex lasiocarpa) or coastal sedge (C. exilis). Species that help to differentiate APn91c from the other types in APn91 include bog willow, three-leaved false Solomon’s seal (Smilacina trifolia), creeping sedge (C. chordorrhiza), sparse-fruited sedge (C. tenuiflora), and Labrador tea (Ledum groenlandicum). Species characteristic of wet hollows are often present, including white beak rush (Rhynchospora alba), scheuchzeria, lead-colored sedge (C. livida), and intermediate bladderwort (Utricularia intermedia). APn91c is associated with both patterned ribbed fens and featureless peatland water tracks in large peatlands and is divided into two subtypes on the basis of features of the peat surface. Description is based on summary of vegetation data from 48 plots.

units.name: Flark Subtype
units.text: Graminoid-dominated fens characterized by distinct linear peat-bottom pools, or “flarks,” that support species such as white beak rush (Rhynchospora alba), spatulate-leaved sundew (Drosera intermedia), lead-colored sedge (Carex livida), bog rush (Juncus stygius), and horned bladderwort (Utricularia cornuta). APn91c2 is best developed in interiors of well-developed water tracks in large glacial lakebed peatlands (usually in association with rich or poor shrub fens), although subtle pool development can also occur in smaller peatlands in the northeastern part of the state. CTn11a is the most common dry cliff type in the North Shore Highlands and much of the Border Lakes subsections in NSU. Early goldenrod is present on most occurrences and red pines are often present on cliff tops. On cliffs in the Rove Landtype Association in the eastern Border Lakes Subsection, CTn11a often occurs as cap of erosion-resistant diabase above a more erodible layer of shale, argillite, or graywacke (see CTn11b below). A southern outlier of CTn11a is present along the St. Croix River at Taylors Falls in WSU.

Characteristic vascular plants include northern and Appalachian firmoss (and hybrids), harebell, and the rare plants smooth woodsia and encrusted saxifrage. CTn32a represents the most common mesic cliff type in the North Shore Highlands and much of the Border Lakes subsections in NSU. On cliffs in the Rove Landtype Association in the eastern Border Lakes Subsection, CTn32a often occurs as a cap of erosion-resistant diabase above a more erodible layer of shale, argillite, or graywacke (see CTn32b).

The lower parts of the Rove Formation and upper parts of the underlying Gunflint Iron Formation tend to be calcareous. The most common bedrock layers include the St. Peter, Jordan, Franconia, Ironton, and Galesville formations. Although cliff faces are often mostly devoid of crevices, lush carpets of bryophytes are present on wetter portions, providing alternative rooting areas for vascular plants. Vascular plants can be quite abundant on bryophyte mats, as is often the case for rare species such as montia (Montia chamissoi).

CTu22.intro: Plant species composition has not been systematically sampled across the range of CTu22, but evidence suggests that composition varies most strongly with exposure to scouring by waves and ice and secondarily to pH and nutrient availability. Therefore, the community types in CTu22 at present are based on degree of exposure to waves and ice, and on broad bedrock categories reflecting bedrock pH and nutrient properties.

units.name: Exposed Mafic Cliff (Lake Superior)
units.text: Open communities on dry, circumneutral to moderately alkaline cliffs composed of basalt, andesite, diabase, or anorthosite. CTu22a is exposed to scouring by waves and ice, which keeps the cliff face largely free of vascular plants, with crustose lichens often the only vegetation present. Orange lichens (Xanthoria spp.) are abundant. Shrubby cinquefoil is often present on upper ledges of the highest cliffs. CTu22a is the most common cliff type along Lake Superior in Minnesota.

units.name: Sheltered Mafic Cliff (Lake Superior)
units.text: Open communities on moist, circumneutral to moderately alkaline cliffs composed of basalt or ferrodiorite on sites protected from wave- and ice-scouring by small, near-shore islands or bedrock points. Unlike CTu22a and CTu22b, which are largely devoid of vascular plants, CTu22c is covered by lush growth of mosses and vascular plants, which root in thick mossy mats as well as in crevices and on ledges, and almost invariably contains arctic-alpine or boreal plant species, including encrusted saxifrage, butterwort (Pinguicula vulgaris), birds-eye primrose (Primula mistassinica), and intermediate sedge (Carex media). CTu22c has been documented at less than a dozen sites in Minnesota.

range.note: CTu22c has been documented at less than a dozen sites in Minnesota.

site: moist, circumneutral to moderately alkaline cliffs composed of basalt or ferrodiorite
sites protected from wave- and ice-scouring by small, near-shore islands or bedrock points
